# Catalog Description

CSIS-106 / DATA-110: Introduction to Exploratory Data Analysis and Visualization
3 credit(s)

Data Science and analytics is an emerging field concerned with gathering, organizing, analyzing and visualizing large collections of information in order to extract actionable knowledge, i.e. to make decisions. This course is a basic introduction to the subject. Students will learn to identify data problems and to gather and analyze data using a suitable programming language such as R or Python. The coursework is aimed to help students to solve real world data problems obtained from a “subject matter expert”, i.e. a client who needs assistance with making data-driven decision in his/her field. No previous programming experience is necessary.

Prerequisite(s): None

# Grading

Your grade will be based on several components, described in more detail below:

| Component                 | Weight |
| ------------------------- | -----: |
| Pre-class assignments         |     8% |
| Notebook activities       |    20% |
| Concept Checks (4)        |    12% |
| Guided Data Investigation |    15% |
| Test 1                    |    10% |
| Test 2                    |    10% |
| Final Data Investigation  |    25% |




* Pre-class assignments (including zybook exercises)
* Notebook activities - these will usually be started in class.  If you are not able to finish the notebook during class time, you are responsible for finishing them outside of class (I will provide instructions and deadlines).
* Concept Checks - these are smaller quizzes on specific topics
* Guided Data Investigation - this will be our midterm project, and it will be a encapsulate the full data science cycle.
* Tests - we will have two in-class written examinations.  These will be on paper, and the questions will emphasize interpretation, tracing, debugging, visualization choices, and reasoning. You may be asked to interpret code, predict program output, identify bugs, critique visualizations, or explain why one analytical approach is more appropriate than another.
* Final data investigation project

# Final Project

The semester culminates in an independent data investigation.

You will select a dataset, formulate a question, analyze the data using the techniques developed throughout the course, and communicate your findings through a reproducible Google Colab notebook and a short presentation.

The project is not a separate experience from the rest of the course—it is the same process that you will have practiced repeatedly throughout the semester, applied independently to a question that interests you.

# Attendance

Because this is an active-learning course, attendance and participation are important.

Most class meetings are built around collaborative notebook activities that cannot be fully replicated outside the classroom. Missing class means missing opportunities to ask questions, receive feedback, and learn from your classmates.

If illness, athletics, or another unavoidable circumstance prevents you from attending class, please let me know as soon as possible.

# Late Work

Notebook activities and problem sets are designed to help you keep pace with the course.

Extensions are available when requested **before** the deadline or when unexpected circumstances arise. Communication is important—please contact me early if you are having difficulty completing an assignment.

---

# Collaboration

Discussion and collaboration are encouraged.

You are welcome to work with classmates on notebook activities unless an assignment explicitly states otherwise. Some activities will specifically ask you to work with a partner.

Collaboration can include discussing ideas, comparing approaches, helping one another interpret error messages, and talking through debugging strategies.

However, every student must submit work that reflects **their own understanding**. Unless you are completing a shared assignment with an assigned partner, you should not simply copy another student's code or written responses.

You should be able to explain the purpose of every line of code you submit, the choices you made in your analysis, and the conclusions you drew from the data.

---

# Artificial Intelligence

Modern scientists, engineers, and data scientists increasingly use AI tools as part of their workflow.

You are encouraged to use AI to help you

* understand programming concepts
* interpret error messages and debug code
* explore alternative approaches
* ask questions about data or methods
* improve the clarity of your writing

AI should support your learning—not replace it.

You are responsible for understanding every line of code and every statement that you submit. You should be able to explain what your code does, why you used a particular approach, and how your results support your conclusions.

When AI contributes substantially to your work, acknowledge how you used it. This can be done in a Markdown cell in your notebook or, when appropriate, in a code comment.

---

# Sources & Attribution

Data science rarely happens without outside resources. Documentation, textbooks, examples, online references, open-source code, and AI tools are all legitimate resources for learning and problem solving.

When you copy, adapt, or substantially rely on code, text, ideas, or other material from an outside source, **acknowledge the source**.

In a computational notebook, this can be done in several ways:

* include a citation or link in a Markdown cell
* add a comment near adapted code identifying the source
* include the source in the notebook's **References & Data Sources** section
* briefly describe how an AI tool contributed to the work

You do not need to cite ordinary Python syntax or techniques that have become part of your own working knowledge. The goal is to make it clear when someone else's work made a meaningful contribution to your analysis.

Regardless of where code comes from, **you are responsible for understanding any code that you submit**.

---

# Academic Integrity

Academic honesty is essential in this course.

Submitted work should reflect your own understanding, except when an assignment explicitly asks you to produce shared work with a partner or group.

Using outside resources is not inherently a violation of academic integrity. Using code, ideas, or other material without appropriate attribution, copying another student's work, or submitting work that you cannot explain are inconsistent with the goals of the course and may constitute academic dishonesty.

In particular:

* do not submit another student's code or written work as your own
* do not allow another person or an AI tool to complete an assignment for you
* acknowledge outside sources when they contribute substantially to your work
* be prepared to explain the code, analysis, and conclusions that you submit

If you are unsure whether a particular kind of collaboration or outside assistance is appropriate, ask.

Learning from examples, documentation, classmates, mistakes, and debugging is expected. The goal is to become increasingly capable of solving problems and reasoning with data independently.
